sec: Classical brain lesion signs and acromegaly treatment

items.q: Match the classical radiological sign to its corresponding intracranial lesion — 1) Ring-enhancing lesion 2) Notochordal remnant with clivus destruction 3) Calcification, bony hyperostosis and pneumosinus dilatations 4) Large lobulated suprasellar mass in 3rd ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus … A) Brain abscess B) Chordoma C) Meningioma D) Germinoma
items.exp: Brain abscess is ring-enhancing; chordoma is a notochordal remnant with clivus destruction; meningioma shows hyperostosis/pneumosinus dilatations; germinoma causes obstructive hydrocephalus in the 3rd ventricle. (Book p951)

items.q: Which imaging features are classically linked with Rathke's cleft cyst?
opts: Claw sign, posterior ledge sign, and intracystic dot/nodule sign
Popcorn appearance on T2 weighted images
items.exp: Rathke's cleft cyst demonstrates the claw sign, posterior ledge sign, and nodule inside / dot sign. (Book p951)

items.q: What is the reported surgical success / biochemical remission rate for transsphenoidal resection of a GH-secreting microadenoma?
items.exp: Surgical resection of a GH microadenoma achieves an 80% success rate. (Book p951)

items.q: What is the surgical success / biochemical cure rate for a GH-secreting macroadenoma?
items.exp: Surgical resection achieves a 50% success rate in GH macroadenomas. (Book p951)

items.q: What is the primary surgical procedure of choice for definitive treatment of acromegaly?
items.exp: The surgery of choice for acromegaly is transsphenoidal hypophysectomy. (Book p951)

items.q: Following surgical resection for acromegaly, a post-operative nadir GH level that is ___ signifies a good success rate and biochemical cure.
items.exp: An undetectable post-operative GH level indicates good surgical success. (Book p951)

items.q: A 48-year-old male with persistent GH elevation following transsphenoidal surgery has persistent tumor on MRI after 3 months. If he is medically unfit for repeat surgery, what is the best alternative intervention?
items.exp: In relapsed or persistent acromegaly where the patient is unfit for surgery, Gamma Knife stereotactic radiotherapy is indicated. (Book p951)

items.q: Match the medical agent for acromegaly to its route of administration — 1) Octreotide 2) Lanreotide 3) Pasireotide … A) Subcutaneous B) Subcutaneous C) Intramuscular
items.exp: Octreotide is subcutaneous, Lanreotide is subcutaneous, and Pasireotide is intramuscular. (Book p951)

items.q: Which pharmacological agent acts as a competitive growth hormone receptor antagonist?
items.exp: Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist. (Book p951)

items.q: A patient with acromegaly is treated with pegvisomant. At follow-up, serum IGF-1 levels have completely normalized, but circulating serum growth hormone levels are elevated. This paradoxical rise in GH is explained by:
opts: Loss of negative feedback inhibition by reduced IGF-1 on the pituitary
Pegvisomant cross-reacting on standard GH immunoassays
Malignant transformation of the residual adenoma
Direct agonism of pegvisomant on somatotroph receptors
items.exp: Pegvisomant blocks peripheral GH receptors; as IGF-1 falls, loss of negative feedback causes circulating GH levels to increase. (Book p951)

items.q: Which drug is NOT used in the medical management of acromegaly?
items.exp: Acromegaly medical therapy includes somatostatin analogs, dopamine agonists, and pegvisomant; metyrapone is used for Cushing syndrome. (Book p951)

items.q: Assess somatostatin analogs in acromegaly: I They bind somatostatin receptor subtypes SST2 through SST5. II Pasireotide has particularly high binding affinity across multiple SST receptor subtypes.
opts: Both I and II are true
Both I and II are false
items.exp: Somatostatin analogs target SST2 to SST5 receptors, with pasireotide showing broad high-affinity receptor binding. (Book p951)
